title: Matteo Ricci
hook: a Jesuit in China who dressed as a scholar and made friends through maps and clocks

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kateri Tekakwitha, praying at a cross cut into bark. Your line was the lily of the Mohawks.

Visitors keep crowding into one house in a Chinese city. They've come to see a map of the whole world, drawn in Chinese characters, hanging on the wall, and to hear a mechanical clock tick and strike the hour. The man who brought them is an Italian in the robes of a Chinese scholar, speaking Chinese and quoting the Chinese classics. He has come to talk about Christ. But he has decided not to start there. He'll start with friendship, and with what his hosts already love: learning.

Matteo Ricci was a Jesuit priest, of the order of Ignatius and Francis Xavier you met earlier in this block. He went to China, and the accounts say he first dressed the way Buddhist monks did, thinking that was how religious teachers looked there. Then he learned that the teachers his hosts looked up to were the scholars, the readers of Confucius. So he changed his clothes, and more than his clothes. He studied the classics until he could quote them, and took a Chinese name. He made his world map in Chinese, and worked with a Chinese scholar named Xu Guangqi to put a Greek geometry book into Chinese. Xu was baptized too. Ricci also wrote a little book on friendship, a collection of sayings about what a friend is, in Chinese, for Chinese readers. And he wrote about God using words and ideas his readers already had, arguing that the old Chinese classics already knew of a Lord of Heaven. Paul said something like it about his own work: "I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." Not everyone agreed with Ricci. After his death, Catholics argued long and hard over how far that kind of meeting could go, especially over honoring ancestors. Some saw wise respect. Some saw too much given away. But his starting point is our line. Jesus says to his disciples in John's Gospel: "I have called you friends." Ricci tried to begin there.
screen: `A MAP, A CLOCK, A GEOMETRY BOOK.`

segments.voice: Think of one person whose family, language or country is different from yours, and what they love: a food, a festival, a kind of music, a saying their grandmother used. Pick one thing you've never asked them about. If you pray, hold them before God by name; if you don't, just wish them well.
Matteo Ricci. An Italian Jesuit in China who took a Chinese name, wore a scholar's robes, made a world map and a book on friendship, and tried to speak of God in his hosts' own words.
Your line: friendship first. Talk of Christ came after, for Ricci. Day nine hundred eight.

howItsDone: Christians who work across cultures often read Ricci's life as a lesson in learning a language and a culture before speaking, and Catholics in China and Italy remember him in their own ways.

chat.meaning: Ricci learned Chinese, wore a scholar's robes and wrote a book on friendship. He spoke of God in words his readers already had.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or counts given. Monk's robes then scholar's robes, the world map, the clocks, the Euclid translation with Xu Guangqi, Xu's baptism and the book on friendship are standard in the Ricci accounts; confirm.
'Arguing that the old Chinese classics already knew of a Lord of Heaven' summarizes The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven (Tianzhu shiyi); confirm the framing.
The Chinese Rites controversy is described only as a long Catholic argument after his death; confirm wording.
